title: The AI Product Landscape: Models, APIs, RAG, and Fine-Tuning
monthTitle: AI Literacy and LLM Foundations for PMs
summary: This lesson gives AI PMs a practical map of the AI product landscape: foundation models, hosted APIs, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and fine-tuning. You'll learn the trade-offs of each approach across cost, latency, accuracy, control, and maintenance, and practice choosing the right pattern for a given use case in a structured comparison brief.
objectives: Distinguish foundation models, hosted model APIs, RAG, and fine-tuning, and explain what problem each solves
Compare build-vs-buy options across cost, latency, data control, accuracy, and maintenance trade-offs
Match common use cases (e.g. Q&A over docs, brand voice, domain knowledge) to the appropriate architectural pattern
Identify when RAG, fine-tuning, or both are needed versus prompt engineering alone
Draft a one-page comparison brief that justifies an architecture recommendation to stakeholders

quiz.q: A support team wants a chatbot to answer questions using their constantly-updated help center articles, with citations. Which approach fits best?
options: Fine-tune a model on the help articles
Hosted API with RAG over the help center
Self-host an open model with no retrieval
Prompt engineering alone with no data access
quiz.why: The knowledge is proprietary and frequently changing and needs citations — RAG retrieves current content at query time without retraining, unlike fine-tuning which goes stale and can't cite sources.

options: Teach the model new, frequently-changing facts
Shape consistent tone, format, or narrow-task behavior
Eliminate the need for any evaluation
quiz.why: Fine-tuning changes behavior — style, format, narrow tasks. It's unreliable for teaching facts (use RAG) and doesn't remove the need for evaluation.

quiz.q: Which approach generally offers the fastest time to ship for an MVP?
quiz.why: Calling a hosted API with prompt engineering requires no infrastructure or training and can produce a working product in days.

quiz.q: When is self-hosting an open model most justified?
options: When you want the fastest possible MVP
When data residency, privacy, regulation, or high-volume economics require it
Whenever you need the model to cite sources
quiz.why: Self-hosting trades higher operational cost for maximum control — justified by privacy, regulatory, residency, or large-scale cost reasons, not speed.

quiz.q: In one or two sentences, explain the 'knowledge vs behavior' rule for choosing between RAG and fine-tuning.
quiz.answer: Use RAG when the model needs to know new or changing facts, since it retrieves your data at query time; use fine-tuning when the model needs to behave a certain way, such as tone, format, or a narrow task. They solve different problems and are often combined.
quiz.why: This captures the core heuristic: RAG injects knowledge, fine-tuning shapes behavior, and prompt engineering should be tried first for light steering.

quiz.q: Name two 'hidden' costs an AI PM should include in a comparison brief beyond per-token price.
quiz.answer: Evaluation pipelines, monitoring, ongoing maintenance/retraining, infrastructure/ops, and vendor risk are all valid examples.
quiz.why: Total cost of ownership includes evals, monitoring, retraining stale fine-tunes or RAG indexes, and infrastructure — ignoring these leads to bad build-vs-buy decisions.

body_markdown:
## Why this matters

As an AI PM, one of your earliest and most consequential decisions is *how* you'll deliver intelligence: which model, hosted or self-managed, and which architectural pattern wraps around it. Get this wrong and you over-spend, under-deliver on accuracy, or build something you can't maintain. This lesson gives you a decision framework, not deep ML theory.

## The four building blocks

### 1. Foundation models
Large pre-trained models (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral) trained on broad data. They are the raw engine. You rarely train one yourself — that costs millions. Your choice is which one to *use* and *how*.

### 2. Hosted model APIs (buy)
You call a provider's model over an API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Bedrock). You pay per token. Fast to ship, no infra, always-improving models, but you give up some data control and depend on a vendor.

### 3. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
You keep your own knowledge in a vector database (or search index), retrieve relevant chunks at query time, and inject them into the prompt. The model 'reads' your data without being retrained. Best for **fresh, proprietary, or frequently-changing knowledge** and when you need citations.

### 4. Fine-tuning
You further train a base model on your examples so it internalizes a **style, format, or narrow task**. Good for consistent tone, structured outputs, or classification at scale. It does *not* reliably teach new facts and must be redone when data changes.

## The mental model: knowledge vs behavior

- Need the model to **know new facts**? → RAG (or tools/APIs).
- Need the model to **behave a certain way** (tone, format, task)? → Fine-tuning.
- Need just a little steering? → **Prompt engineering** first — it's free and instant.
- These combine: many production systems use a hosted API + RAG + light prompt engineering, and add fine-tuning only when justified.

## Build vs buy spectrum

| Approach | Time to ship | Cost profile | Data control | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted API + prompting | Days | Per-token, low upfront | Lower (vendor) | MVPs, general tasks |
| Hosted API + RAG | Weeks | Per-token + infra for retrieval | Medium | Q&A over your docs |
| Fine-tuned hosted model | Weeks–months | Training + serving cost | Medium | Consistent style/format/task |
| Self-hosted open model | Months | High infra + ops | Highest | Privacy, scale economics, regulation |

## Decision heuristics

1. **Start cheap and fast.** Try prompt engineering on a hosted API before anything else.
2. **Add RAG when answers depend on your data** or need to be current and cited.
3. **Fine-tune for behavior, not knowledge** — and only after prompting plateaus.
4. **Self-host when** data residency, privacy, regulatory, or high-volume cost reasons demand it.
5. **Watch total cost of ownership:** eval pipelines, monitoring, retraining, and vendor risk, not just per-token price.

## The comparison brief (your deliverable)

A one-pager that, for a specific use case, lists: the problem and success metric, 2–3 candidate approaches, a trade-off table (cost, latency, accuracy, data control, maintenance), risks, and a recommendation with rationale. This is the artifact you'll bring to engineering and leadership.

## Common pitfalls

- Jumping to fine-tuning to 'teach facts' — usually the wrong tool; use RAG.
- Ignoring evaluation: you can't compare approaches without a test set and metrics.
- Underestimating maintenance: RAG indexes go stale; fine-tunes need re-training; vendors change models.
- Optimizing per-token cost while ignoring engineering and ops cost.

slides.title: The AI Product Landscape
slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll map the AI product landscape so that as a product manager you can confidently choose how to deliver intelligence in your product. We'll cover foundation models, hosted APIs, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning, and finish with a comparison brief you can take to your team.

slides.title: The four building blocks
bullets: Foundation models: the raw engine (GPT-4, Claude, Llama)
Hosted APIs: rent the model, pay per token
RAG: inject your data at query time
Fine-tuning: train behavior into the model
slides.narration: There are four building blocks you need to know. Foundation models are the large pre-trained engines you almost never train yourself. Hosted APIs let you rent those models per token. RAG retrieves your own data and feeds it into the prompt. And fine-tuning further trains a model to behave a certain way. Almost every AI product is a combination of these.

slides.title: Buy first: hosted APIs
bullets: Fastest path to a working product — days, not months
No infrastructure to run; models keep improving
Per-token cost, low upfront investment
Trade-offs: vendor dependency, less data control
slides.narration: For most teams, the right starting point is buying — calling a hosted API. You get a working product in days, no GPUs to manage, and the provider keeps upgrading the model for free. You pay per token. The trade-offs are vendor lock-in and giving up some control over where your data goes. Start here unless you have a strong reason not to.

slides.title: RAG: give the model your knowledge
bullets: Store docs as embeddings in a vector database
Retrieve relevant chunks per query, add to prompt
Great for proprietary, fresh, or citable knowledge
No retraining when your data changes
slides.narration: RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, is how you make a general model answer questions about your specific data. You chunk and embed your documents into a vector store, retrieve the most relevant pieces at query time, and put them in the prompt. It's ideal when answers depend on your proprietary or frequently-changing content, and when you need citations. Crucially, updating your data is just updating the index — no retraining.

slides.title: Fine-tuning: shape behavior
bullets: Train base model on your examples
Best for tone, format, and narrow tasks
Poor at teaching new facts — that's RAG's job
Must be re-trained when requirements change
slides.narration: Fine-tuning takes a base model and trains it further on your examples so it consistently produces a certain style, format, or completes a narrow task. It's excellent for brand voice or structured outputs. But it's the wrong tool for teaching facts — those get stale and are better handled by RAG. Remember: fine-tuning changes behavior, RAG changes knowledge.

slides.title: Knowledge vs behavior
bullets: Need new facts? → RAG or tools
Need a consistent way of acting? → Fine-tune
Need light steering? → Prompt engineering first
Production often combines all three
slides.narration: Here's the mental model that cuts through the confusion. If you need the model to know new facts, use RAG. If you need it to behave a certain way, fine-tune. If you just need a little steering, prompt engineering is free and instant — always try it first. Real production systems frequently combine a hosted API, RAG, and prompting, adding fine-tuning only when prompting plateaus.

slides.title: Build-vs-buy spectrum
bullets: API + prompting: days, lowest effort, MVPs
API + RAG: weeks, your docs, medium control
Fine-tuned model: weeks–months, consistent behavior
Self-hosted open model: highest control, highest ops cost
slides.narration: Think of options on a spectrum. A hosted API with prompting ships in days and suits MVPs. Adding RAG takes weeks and unlocks question-answering over your documents. Fine-tuning adds consistent behavior but more effort. At the far end, self-hosting an open model gives maximum data control and possibly better economics at scale, but you own all the infrastructure and operations. Move right only when there's a clear reason.

slides.title: Decision heuristics
bullets: Start cheap and fast: prompt on a hosted API
Add RAG when answers depend on your data
Fine-tune for behavior, after prompting plateaus
Self-host for privacy, regulation, or scale economics
Budget for evals, monitoring, and maintenance
slides.narration: To apply this, follow a few heuristics. Start cheap and fast with prompting on a hosted API. Add RAG when answers depend on your data or need to be current. Reach for fine-tuning only for behavior, and only after prompting plateaus. Self-host when privacy, regulation, or volume economics demand it. And always budget for the hidden costs — evaluation pipelines, monitoring, and ongoing maintenance — not just per-token price.
